# Overlapping dot plots {#sec-overlapping-dot-plots}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_goosebumps(
    base_size = 15))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_goosebumps()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_goosebumps()`, modeled on the Goosebumps books: a black background, a slime green frame and title, a dark purple plot area, slime green, purple, pale green, orchid, and moss marks, and a Trattatello title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1992)
goosebumps_readers <- tibble(
  student_id = 1:120,
  grade = rep(c("3rd grade", "4th grade", "5th grade"), each = 40)) |>
  mutate(grade = factor(grade,
           levels = c("3rd grade", "4th grade", "5th grade")),
         books_read = rpois(n(), lambda = c(`3rd grade` = 3, `4th grade` = 6,
                                            `5th grade` = 9)[as.character(grade)]))
labs_ovrlp_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Goosebumps books read",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "40 students in each grade, one school year",
  x = "Books read",
  fill = "Grade")
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot <- ggplot(data = goosebumps_readers,
    aes(x = books_read,
        fill = grade)) +
  geom_dotplot(
    method = "histodot",
    binwidth = 1,
    dotsize = 0.4,
    binpositions = "all",
    stackgroups = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot +
  labs_ovrlp_dotplot
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a categorical variable**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (count) variable**
:::

::::

## Description

A [dot plot](dot_plots.qmd) shows each number in the data as a dot along one axis. Overlapping dot plots put the dots for every group in the same graph, so we can compare the form the numbers take from one group to the next.[^dist-shape]

A [histogram](histograms.qmd) cuts the `x` axis into boxes and shows how many numbers fall in each box, and a [frequency polygon](frequency_polygons.qmd) shows where numbers fall, using points joined by straight lines. `method` picks the boxes the dots go in: `"histodot"` uses boxes that are all the same size, like a histogram, and `"dotdensity"` (used if we don't pick one) moves each box to where its dots fall. `binpositions` lines up the boxes for all the groups.[^arguments]

## Set up


::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages]
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
*Goosebumps* was a set of books by R.L. Stine, written to make kids feel fear. In the middle of the 1990s, these books were all over, and older kids often read more of them, and fast. A grade is one year of school, and kids in the same grade are about the same age. We'll make up[^simulate] how many Goosebumps books 40 students in each of three grades read in one school year. `rpois()` picks each student's number from a [rule made for how many times something happens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution),[^poisson] with a different mean (`lambda`) for each grade: 3, 6, and 9 books. Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 120 students every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1992) # same 120 students every time the code runs
goosebumps_readers <- tibble(
  student_id = 1:120, # 120 different students, one row each
  grade = rep(c("3rd grade", "4th grade", "5th grade"), each = 40) # 40 students per grade
  ) |>
  mutate(
    grade = factor(grade,
      levels = c("3rd grade", "4th grade", "5th grade")), # youngest to oldest
    books_read = rpois(n(),
      lambda = c(`3rd grade` = 3, `4th grade` = 6, # average books read
                 `5th grade` = 9)[as.character(grade)] # (looked up for each grade)
      )
    )
dplyr::glimpse(goosebumps_readers)
```
:::

## Distribution

A pile is a set of dots, one on top of the next. Dot plots work well for small whole numbers:[^counts] every student gets one dot, and every number of books gets its own pile. With the dots for all three grades in the same piles, we can see two things change from grade to grade: where the middle of the piles is, and how far the piles run out to each side.[^spread] Below we'll move from the students, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula]

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten students (all in 3rd grade).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(goosebumps_readers$books_read, 10)
```
:::

These 3rd graders read between two and five books. The variance is a number for how far the numbers fall from the mean. The numbers below[^summary] compare the mean and variance for each grade. For whole numbers like these, the variance gets bigger as the mean gets bigger, so the numbers for the older students fall farther from each other.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
goosebumps_readers |> 
  group_by(grade) |> 
  summarise(mean = mean(books_read), variance = var(books_read),
            min = min(books_read), max = max(books_read))
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The graph below gives each grade its own small graph,[^facets] one above the next (with `facet_wrap()`), and the broken lines[^dashed] mark the mean we gave each grade in `rpois()`. The 3rd grade piles are high and close together near three books, and the 5th grade piles are low and run from three books to well past 12.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| fig-asp: 1.4
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
ggplot(goosebumps_readers, aes(x = books_read, fill = grade)) + 
  geom_dotplot(method = "histodot", binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.55,
    show.legend = FALSE) + 
  geom_vline(data = tibble(grade = factor(c("3rd grade", "4th grade", 
      "5th grade")), lambda = c(3, 6, 9)), 
    aes(xintercept = lambda), linetype = "dashed", color = "#F2E8CF") + 
  facet_wrap(~ grade, ncol = 1) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) + 
  labs(x = "Books read")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Each grade's numbers come from a [rule made for how many times something happens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution):[^poisson-name]

$$
X_{\text{grade}} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{\text{grade}}), \quad \lambda = (3, 6, 9)
$$

For this rule, the variance is the same as the mean ($\lambda$), so how far the numbers usually fall from the mean[^sd] is $\sqrt{\lambda}$: about 1.7 books for 3rd graders and 3 books for 5th graders. By the rule, making the mean three times bigger only makes the piles $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.7$ times wider. In our made up students the number is a little bigger (1.4 books for 3rd graders and 3.3 books for 5th graders, about 2.3 times wider), but the 5th grade piles are still not three times wider. When we pile the three grades into one dot plot, the middle grade shares numbers with the grades on both sides of it.[^overlap] All three colors already share the piles at 3, 4, 5, and 7 books. Try giving the three grades means that are closer together in `rpois()`, and more piles will hold all three colors.


## Grammar

::: {.column-margin}
- [`binwidth`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_dotplot.html) = *When method is "histodot", this specifies bin width. Defaults to 1/30 of the range of the data*

- [`binpositions`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_dotplot.html) = *"all" determines positions of the bins with all the data taken together; this is used for aligning dot stacks across multiple groups.*
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

  -   Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()`

  -   Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data`

  -   Put `books_read` on the `x` axis

  -   Give each `grade` its own color with `fill`

  -   Inside `geom_dotplot`, set `method` to `"histodot"`, `binwidth` to `1` (one pile for each number of books), `dotsize` to `0.4` (so the highest pile fits), `binpositions` to `"all"`, and `stackgroups` to `TRUE` (so each grade's dots go on top of the last grade's dots instead of covering them)[^stackgroups]

  -   Take away the numbers on the `y` axis with `scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)`, because they run from 0 to 1 and do not stand for a number of students

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_ovrlp_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Goosebumps books read",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "40 students in each grade, one school year",
  x = "Books read",
  fill = "Grade")
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot <- ggplot(data = goosebumps_readers,
    aes(x = books_read,
        fill = grade)) +
  geom_dotplot(
    method = "histodot",
    binwidth = 1,
    dotsize = 0.4,
    binpositions = "all",
    stackgroups = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot +
  labs_ovrlp_dotplot
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_ovrlp_dot_plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_ovrlp_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Goosebumps books read",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "40 students in each grade, one school year",
  x = "Books read",
  fill = "Grade")
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot <- ggplot(data = goosebumps_readers,
    aes(x = books_read,
        fill = grade)) +
  geom_dotplot(
    method = "histodot",
    binwidth = 1,
    dotsize = 0.4,
    binpositions = "all",
    stackgroups = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)
ggp2_ovrlp_dotplot +
  labs_ovrlp_dotplot
```

[^dist-shape]: Overlapping dot plots display the distribution of a numeric variable across the levels of a categorical variable.

[^arguments]: The `method` and `binpositions` arguments. With `"histodot"`, the bins have a fixed width; with `"dotdensity"`, the bin centers follow the data.

[^packages]: Install and load the packages.

[^simulate]: Simulate.

[^poisson]: A Poisson distribution, a common model for counts.

[^seed]: Setting the random seed.

[^counts]: Small counts.

[^spread]: Where the stacks are centered, and how spread out they are.

[^formula]: The formula.

[^summary]: Summary statistics: the mean, variance, minimum, and maximum for each grade.

[^facets]: A facet.

[^dashed]: Dashed lines.

[^poisson-name]: A Poisson distribution.

[^sd]: The standard deviation.

[^overlap]: The middle grade overlaps both of its neighbors.

[^labels]: Labels.

[^stackgroups]: With `stackgroups = TRUE`, the groups stack on top of each other instead of overplotting.
